ROLE

You are a motion-graphics director and documentary scriptwriter. Create a polished, animated
explainer video titled "The History of Google: From a Dorm Project to the AI Era (1996–2026)".
It will be published on YouTube and X, so it must hook viewers in the first 3 seconds and keep
the pace high throughout.
DELIVERABLES
Main video: 16:9, 1080p (4K if possible), 2-3 minutes, 30 fps.
VISUAL STYLE
Clean, modern flat motion graphics with smooth easing (no stiff linear moves). Think
premium tech explainer, not a slideshow.
Palette built on Google's four colours (blue, red, yellow, green) on white or dark backgrounds.

Recurring motif: each chapter opens with a search bar where the year is typed in, a cursor
blinks, and "Enter" launches the scene.
Use kinetic typography for key numbers and dates. Use parallax, masked reveals, and
light particle accents. No cheesy stock transitions.

Show the period's interfaces as stylised recreations: the 1998 homepage, the early Gmail
inbox, the first Android phone, the Chrome browser window, and the Gemini chat.
Include a running year counter in a corner so viewers always know where they are.
LOGO RULE (most important)
Whenever a year is on screen, show the Google logo that was actually in use at that time. Do not redraw, restyle, or approximate them. Transitions between
eras should be a signature "logo morph" moment where the old logo dissolves into the next one.

1997–Sep 1998: original prototype "Google" logo (from Sep 15, 1997)
Sep 28–Oct 29, 1998: Baskerville Bold logo with a green "G"
Oct 30, 1998–May 30, 1999: logo with the exclamation mark ("Google!")
May 31, 1999–May 2010: the Ruth Kedar serif logo with drop shadow
May 2010–Sep 2013: refreshed serif logo with a softer shadow
Sep 2013–Aug 2015: flat serif logo, no shadow
Sep 1, 2015 onward: sans-serif wordmark plus the four-colour segmented "G" icon
May 2025: gradient "G" icon debuts on Search; Sep 2025: becomes the company-wide "G"

May 2026: slightly refined wordmark with brighter hues
Finale: a rapid "evolution" sequence of every logo in order, ending on the current one.
STORY STRUCTURE (if you need any for reference)
0:00 Hook: "In 1998 Google ran out of a garage. Today, billions of people use it every day.
Here's how it happened." (Open on the 1998 logo glitch-morphing into today's logo.)
1995–1997, The Stanford dorm room: Larry Page and Sergey Brin meet; BackRub and PageRank
rank pages by their links; the name comes from "googol" (a 1 followed by 100 zeros);
http://google.com is registered in 1997.
1998, The garage: the $100,000 cheque from Andy Bechtolsheim made out to "Google Inc."
before the company existed; incorporation in September 1998; Susan Wojcicki's garage in
Menlo Park; the first Doodle (Burning Man, 1998).
1999–2004, The money machine: venture funding, AdWords (2000), Gmail launches on April 1,
2004 (people thought it was a joke), and the IPO in August 2004.
2005–2008, Beyond search: Google Maps and Google Earth, buying Android (2005) and YouTube
(2006), Chrome and the first Android phone (2008).
2014–2017, The AI bet: DeepMind acquisition, AlphaGo beating Lee Sedol (2016), the
"AI-first" declaration, and Google researchers publishing the Transformer paper (2017)
that powers today's chatbots.
2015–2019, Becoming Alphabet: the Alphabet restructure, the new logo, and Sundar Pichai
becoming CEO of Google (2015) and then Alphabet (2019).
2020–2024, Pressure and competition: antitrust cases, including a 2024 US court ruling on
search; ChatGPT's arrival; Bard in 2023, rebranded as Gemini.
2025–2026, The agentic era: the gradient "G," Gemini 3.x models, and the "agentic Gemini
era" framing at I/O 2026.
Outro: the logo evolution montage, then the question "What will Google look like at 30?"
and a subscribe/follow call to action.
TONE AND AUDIO
Confident, curious, fast-paced narrator. Short sentences. One surprising fact per chapter.
Upbeat electronic score that builds; subtle whooshes and keyboard-click sound design on the
search-bar transitions. Duck the music under the voiceover.
ACCURACY RULES

Every date and number on screen must be factually correct. Verify everything
against a current source before using it.
Do not invent statistics.
Include a small end-card disclaimer at the bottom: "Not affiliated with or endorsed by Google. Logos  shown for historical/editorial purposes."
